newsitem.title: UK: Study shows stopping ovaries helps breast cancer.
newsitem.headline: Study shows stopping ovaries helps breast cancer.

text.p: Women suffering from early breast cancer can live longer if the normal function of their ovaries is stopped, an international group of researchers said on Friday.

In a report in the Lancet medical journal the researchers, whose work was coordinated by Britain's Imperial Cancer Research Fund, said using surgery or x-rays to stop the ovaries from working was an effective treatment for early breast cancer in younger women.
"In women aged under 50 with early breast cancer, ablation of functioning ovaries significantly improves long-term survival, at least in the absence of chemotherapy," the researchers said.
They compiled results from 12 clinical trials involving 2,102 premenopausal women who received either surgery or x-ray treatment.
The researchers found that for every 100 women whose ovaries were switched off or removed, an extra six would be alive 15 years later compared to the control group.
Previous medical studies have shown that oestrogen produced by the ovaries is linked to breast cancer and chances of the disease recurring.

"The first report on ovarian ablation, for advanced breast cancer, was published 100 years ago...and nearly 50 years ago the first randomised trial of ovarian ablation for early breast cancer began," Dr Mike Clarke, a coordinator of the report, said in a statement.

"Various studies followed but they were too small to tell doctors much. Only now, by combining results of these 12 trials worldwide, can we give doctors really clear evidence that ablation works," he added.
The research also showed that when ablation is combined with chemotherapy the effect is smaller, probably because chemotheraphy tends to suppress the ovaries already.
Clarke warned that despite the benefits of ablation in cancer treatment, women and their doctors must also consider side-effects.
In addition to loss of fertility, women can face acute menopausal symptoms and may experience long-term effects associated with an early menopause including osteoporosis, or brittle bone disease.
The report called for more studies into the effects of turning off the ovaries when women are receiving other treatments.
Each year about 6,000 women under the age of 50 in Britain and up to 250,000 women worldwide are diagnosed with breast cancer.
